title: Chat app (WhatsApp)
summary: 1:1 and group messaging for 500M daily users: 240M open connections, per-conversation ordering, ticks that never lie, and push for everyone offline.
interviewerPrompt: Let's design a chat app like WhatsApp. People send messages to each other and to groups, and see when their messages were delivered and read. How would you build it?

clarifyingQuestions.question: How many users, and how much do they send?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: 500M daily active users, each sending about 40 messages a day. Assume the evening peak is about twice the daily average.

clarifyingQuestions.question: 1:1 only, or groups too? How big can a group be?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Both. Groups have up to 500 members. Assume about 90% of messages are 1:1 and the rest go to groups with about 10 other members on average.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do we keep message history on the server?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, forever, and a user's phone and laptop must both show the full history in the same order.

clarifyingQuestions.question: What does the sender's tick promise?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: One tick means the server has stored the message durably; it must never be lost after that. Two ticks mean it reached at least one of the recipient's devices; blue means read.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How fast must delivery be?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Under 500 ms end to end to a recipient who is online, at p99. Recipients who are offline get the message when they reconnect, and a mobile push notification wakes them.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does order matter?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Within one conversation, every member's devices must show messages in the same order, and no device may show a gap without knowing it has one. There is no ordering requirement across conversations.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do we need online presence and typing indicators?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Online / last seen, yes. Typing indicators are nice to have. Both may be slightly stale or lost; they are never worth delaying a message for.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Media?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Photos, voice notes and video are allowed, but uploading and storing the bytes is a separate blob service; the message carries a pointer and a key. Focus on text messages.

clarifyingQuestions.question: End-to-end encryption?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Messages should be end-to-end encrypted so the server cannot read them. Understand what that changes in the design; you do not need to design the cryptography.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How are offline users woken up?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Through Apple and Google push services (APNs and FCM). Assume our combined send quota with them is about 100,000 notifications per second.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Multiple devices per user?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes: assume 1.3 devices per user on average (most have only a phone). All of a user's devices receive every message.

deepDiveQuestions: How do you hold 240M open connections, and how does a message find the gateway its recipient is connected to?
How do you guarantee that every device shows a conversation's messages in the same order, with no silent gaps?
How do delivered and read receipts and offline delivery work without losing or duplicating messages?
How do group messages fan out, and how does presence work without flooding the system?
What does end-to-end encryption change in this design?

runChallenge.title: Evening peak with a zone down
runChallenge.description: Run at the 2× evening peak (about 1.16M requests per second: sends, receipts and reconnect syncs) and lose the availability zone holding the most components after 10 s. Senders must still get their tick within 200 ms at p99, with under 0.5% errors and no single point of failure.

commonMistakes: Ordering messages by the sender's device clock, or by server wall-clock timestamps from different machines, so two members of a group see the same conversation in different orders.
Acknowledging the send (one tick) before the message is durably stored, then losing it when a gateway or broker dies.
Sizing the WebSocket tier by messages per second instead of by open connections, which come out at hundreds of thousands per machine and decide the fleet size.
Storing user-to-gateway routing in the gateway that holds the connection, with no shared registry, so nobody else can find where to deliver.
Broadcasting every presence change to every contact, which turns presence into the largest traffic source in the system.
Sending one push notification per message to offline users, which blows through the push providers' quotas within minutes during a busy group chat.
Treating at-least-once delivery as a bug to be eliminated instead of making delivery idempotent with a client-generated message ID.
Claiming end-to-end encryption while also designing server-side search, spam scanning of message text, or server-generated link previews.
